text.en: Plants in the genus Artemesia include sagebrush and wormwood (an ingredient in absinthe). Another species is the source of artemisinin, a potent anti-malarial drug. Used by the Chinese for over a thousand years, artemesinin was "discovered" internationally in the 1980s. Today, the chemical is so widely used that malarial parasites are developing resistance.

text.en: Can a plant lead to war? When the Chinese restricted imports of British goods, the British East India Company balanced the trade deficit by selling opium, grown in India, to Chinese merchants and smugglers. Chinese resistance to the trade led to the 19th-century Opium Wars, and the economic effects of centuries of opium addiction paved the way for the rise of Chinese Communism. Ornamental varieties of opium poppy, low in opiates, are now commonly grown in gardens.

text.en: Used for hundreds of years to treat heart troubles, foxglove was the original source of digitalis, a heart medicine now synthesized in factories. But digitalis is also a potent poison, and eating any part of the foxglove plant can be fatal. Digitalis is a glycoside, one of the most important kinds of plant poisons (and medicines).

text.en: Although grey wolves are fast runners, they are better known for their endurance. Slightly webbed toes allow them to move easily over snow, and scent glands between the toes leave chemical markers behind to inform other wolves of their whereabouts.

text.en: Bears rely mainly on their sense of smell to find food. Their sense of smell is one of the best among mammals.

text.en: Like many other reptiles, lizards have scales and are “cold-blooded,” or ectothermic. Their blood isn’t actually cold, but the animals’ body temperatures depend on the temperature of their environments. That’s why lizards like to sunbathe on rocks.

text.en: Full-grown rabbits and hares look quite similar, but they’re very different at birth. Rabbits are born altricial, meaning they’re naked with closed eyes. Hares are precocial at birth, with fur and open eyes.

text.en: From 1950 to 1970, peregrine falcon populations in Europe and North America crashed due to pesticide poisoning. These birds are now protected in most parts of Canada and the United States, as well as in many other parts of the world.

details.notes: Photo of a peregrine falcon with caption. Photo credit: Ingrid Taylar.

text.en: The order Passeriformes accounts for more than half of all bird species and includes swallows, sparrows, thrushes, wood warblers, and many, many more.

Photo panel with Gray jay. Photo credit: Nigel Tate.

Photo panel with Bewick's wren. Photo credit: Nigel Tate.

text.en: The crow family, Corvidae, includes some of the smartest birds in the world. Ravens mimic the calls of other birds, and captive blue jays have even been known to use tools to gather food!

details.notes: Info panel featuring a Carrion crow egg photo and narrative about Corvidae intelligence. Photo credit: David Gilbar.
Photo of a Steller's jay perched on a branch. Photo credit: Nigel Tate.

details.notes: Header panel for Piciformes / Woodpeckers. 'Inside the cabinet' label visible. Photo of Downy woodpecker, credit Donna Dewhurst.

text.en: Woodpeckers have several traits that set them apart from other bird families, including very long, barbed tongues covered with glue-like saliva. They use these sticky tongues to search tree crevices for unsuspecting insects.

details.notes: Info panel with narrative text about woodpecker tongues. Photo of Red-breasted sapsucker, credit Kevin Cole.
Black panel with no visible text or specimen content. Brown/rust colored bar at bottom.
Photo of Acorn woodpecker bathing in water. Photo credit: Kevin Cole.

details.notes: Header panel for Strigiformes / Owls (variant with different photo). 'Inside the cabinet' label visible. Photo of Great grey owl, credit Scott Liddell.

text.en: The spotted owl is one of the most endangered owls in the world. In Canada, it's only found in southwestern British Columbia, where only eight pairs are still alive in the wild. The spotted owl relies on old-growth forests, few of which still exist in North America.

details.notes: Photo credit: Karen Hollingsworth. Large photograph of a Northern spotted owl with narrative text panel.
Dark/black panel with no visible text or specimen content. Brown/rust strip along bottom edge.
Header panel for Charadriiformes. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet' vertically on left. Photo of a Willet by Nigel Tate. Taxonomy tree shown on upper right.

text.en: The arctic tern boasts one of the most impressive migrations of all birds. Every year, it flies 70,000 kilometres, from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back! Not bad for a bird that weighs just over 100 grams!

details.notes: Photo credit: Sam Judson. Large photograph of an Arctic tern in flight with narrative text panel.
Photo credit: David Gilbar. Label reads 'Common murre (egg)' with scientific name Uria aalge. Shows a single pear-shaped egg with brown markings on white shell.
Dark/black panel with no visible text or specimen content. Brown/rust strip along bottom edge.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Porifera

details.notes: Header panel for Sponges section. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Erika Paradis. Caption: 'Decorated warbonnet, in cloud sponge'.

text.en: Sponges have many different kinds of cells that perform different functions -- some feed, while others protect or reproduce. Unlike other animals, however, sponges do not have true tissues or organ systems.

details.notes: Info panel for Sponges. Photo credit: Jim Patterson. Caption: 'Dead man's finger, Neoesperiopsis sp.'

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Cnidaria

details.notes: Header panel for Corals section. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Commander William Harrigan.

text.en: A coral is really a “city” of millions of small animals, called polyps, building new layers on top of the skeletons of their ancestors. They’re genetically identical, and they’re so integrated that some scientists say a coral could be called a “superorganism.”

details.notes: Info panel for Corals. Photo credit: Albert Kok. Caption: 'Table coral, Acropora pulchra'.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Annelida > Polychaetea > Canalipalpata

specimens.commonName: Red and white Christmas tree worm

details.notes: Header panel for Tube worms section. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Nick Hobgood.

text.en: We don’t normally think of worms as beautiful, but tube worms are indisputably gorgeous. These brightly coloured creatures show off their elaborate headpieces while filter-feeding on the ocean floor.

details.notes: Info panel for Tube worms. Photo credit: John Rix. Caption: 'Duster worm, Eudistylia vancouveri'.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Mollusca > Polyplacophora

details.notes: Header panel for Chitons section. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Colin Bates.

text.en: Chitons can usually be found grazing on algae in the ocean's intertidal zone—the area that's underwater at high tide and exposed to air at low tide. The world's largest chiton, the gumboot chiton, is commonly found in British Columbia.

details.notes: Photo credit: Ron Wolf. Photo shows a gumboot chiton in situ among purple sea urchins.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Mollusca > Gastropoda

text.en: Inside the cabinet

details.notes: Header panel for Gastropoda section. Photo shows a nudibranch (Nudibranchia) on rock. Photo credit: Ryan Cloutier.

text.en: Very early in their lives, gastropods go through a process called torsion, during which the animal twists on itself in such a way that its anus ends up over its head. Torsion allows gastropods to tuck their heads into the opening of their coiled shells for protection.

details.notes: Photo credit: Andy Goryachev. Photo shows two banana slugs.
Photo of tiger slug on black background. Photo credit: Dr. Arthur Anker. No narrative text on this panel.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Mollusca > Gastropoda > Conidae

text.en: Inside the cabinet

details.notes: Header panel for Gastropoda: Conidae section. Photo shows geography cone snails. Photo credit: Ryan Cloutier.

text.en: The hard, tongue-like feeding structure of molluscs, called the radula, comes in many shapes and sizes. The cone snail's poisonous harpoon is actually its radula.

details.notes: Photo of Dall's cone snail in situ among coral. Photo credit: Olin Feurbacher.
Photo shows six cone snail shells of varying patterns displayed against black background. Label reads 'Cone snails (shells)' with 'Conidae' in italics.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Mollusca > Gastropoda > Cypraeidae

Bottom right caption reads 'Cowries (shells) Cypraeidae'. Taxonomy tree terminates at Cypraeidae. Multiple cowrie shell photographs displayed. Orange bar at bottom.

text.en: In living cowries, the beautiful shell is usually hidden under a layer of textured flesh called the mantle.

details.notes: Info panel with photograph of living mole cowry showing mantle. Caption reads 'Mole cowry Cypraea talpa'. Photo credit 'Juuyoh Tanaka'. Text 'Inside the cabinet' visible vertically on left. Orange bar at bottom.

Taxonomy tree terminates at Strombidae. Three conch shell photographs displayed. Orange bar at bottom.

Info panel with photograph of a living strawberry conch. Caption reads 'Strawberry conch Strombus luhuanus'. Photo credit 'Richard Ling'. Text 'Inside the cabinet' visible vertically on left. Orange bar at bottom. No narrative text on this panel.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Cnidaria

details.notes: Header panel reading 'Cnidaria' with common name 'Anemones and jellies'. Text 'Inside the cabinet' visible vertically on left. Bottom right caption reads 'Sea anemone Actiniaria'. Photo credit 'Ryan Cloutier'. Taxonomy tree terminates at Cnidaria. Orange bar at bottom.

text.en: Cnidarians are jelly-like animals with special cells called nematocysts, which they use to capture prey and protect themselves. A nematocyst fires a tiny, harpoon-like thread, which often contains poison to paralyze the cnidarian’s victim.

details.notes: Info panel with photograph of lion's mane jellyfish. Caption reads 'Lion's mane jellyfish Cyanea capillata'. Photo credit 'Travis Shinabarger'. Orange bar at bottom.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Ctenophora

Photo credit 'The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration'. Taxonomy tree terminates at Ctenophora. Orange bar at bottom.

details.notes: Header panel for Platyhelminthes (Flatworms). Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo of Divided flatworm credited to Richard Ling. Taxonomy tree displayed in upper right.

text.en: The highly flattened bodies of flatworms increase surface area to aid breathing and movement. The group contains some of the most striking animals on Earth, from grotesque parasitic tapeworms to beautiful, free-living tropical flatworms.

details.notes: Info panel for Flatworms. Photo of Persian carpet flatworm credited to Richard Ling.
Photo panel showing a tapeworm (Cestoda sp.). Photo credited to Ondrej Zicha. No narrative text on this panel.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Nemertea

details.notes: Header panel for Nemertea (Ribbon worms). Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo of ribbon worm credited to Dr. Arthur Anker. Taxonomy tree displayed in upper right.

text.en: Most ribbon worms are very small, but some species can grow up to 30 metres — making them the longest animals in the world! To feed, a ribbon worm shoots a long appendage, called a proboscis, out of its head and wraps it around its prey.

details.notes: Info panel for Ribbon worms. Photo of Spoon worm (Baseodiscus hemprichii) credited to Dr. Arthur Anker.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Annelida

details.notes: Header panel. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Sheila Byers.

text.en: The annelids include a huge variety of marine segmented worms, as well as land-dwelling species like earthworms and leeches. Although leeches are infamous parasites with powerful suckers, they also contain medically important molecules that stop blood clotting and dilate blood vessels.

details.notes: Info panel for Annelida. Label beneath image reads 'Bloodworm / Glyceridae'. Photo credit: Sheila Byers.

text.en: The bone-eating snot-flower worm feasts on decaying whale bones, part of a whole ecosystem that a whale carcass can support on the ocean floor. Half the worm stays buried inside the bone, and the other half emerges as a pink, flowerlike plume covered in—you guessed it—snot.

details.notes: Info panel for Annelida continued. Photo credit: Adrian Glover.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Ecdysozoa > Arthropoda > Crustacea

details.notes: Header panel. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Ryan Cloutier.

specimens.commonName: Tropical hermit crab inside mollusc shell

text.en: Crustaceans, which include lobsters, krill, and barnacles, are the most widely distributed—and some scientists say the most diverse—group of animals on Earth. Most are marine, though a few, such as wood lice or “pill bugs,” live on land.

details.notes: Info panel for Crustacea. Photo credit: Ryan Cloutier.
Image-only info panel for Crustacea. Label reads 'Woodlice / Porcellio scaber and Oniscus asellus'. No photographer credit visible.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Deuterostomia > Chordata > Urochordata

details.notes: Header panel. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Kevin King.

text.en: A close relative of vertebrates, tunicates (or sea squirts) begin life as free-swimming tadpoles. Eventually, the tadpole settles onto a suitable rock and glues itself to it forever. The adult tunicate grows a thick covering to protect itself from predators and a basket-like organ for filter-feeding.

details.notes: Photo credit: Richard Ling. Image shows yellow/orange sea tulips. Grey rectangle in upper left corner (likely a map/locator graphic).

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Deuterostomia > Echinodermata

details.notes: Header panel for Echinodermata section. Text 'Inside the cabinet' displayed vertically on left. Photo credit: Colin Bates. Grey rectangle in upper left corner.
Photo panel showing dense cluster of ochre stars in purple and orange. Photo credit: Colin Bates. Grey rectangle in upper left corner.

text.en: A sea cucumber can distract predators by gracefully squirting its guts and respiratory organs out through its anus (a process called evisceration). Once it has escaped danger, it can start to rebuild its digestive system.

details.notes: Photo credit: Erika Paradis. Close-up image of red sea cucumber. Grey rectangle in upper left corner.
Photo panel showing red feather star. Photo credit: Richard Ling. Grey rectangle in upper left corner.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Mollusca > Bivalva

details.notes: Header panel for Bivalvia section. Text 'Inside the cabinet' displayed vertically on left. Photo credit: Colin Bates. Taxonomy tree ends with 'Bivalva' as displayed. Grey rectangle in upper left corner.

text.en: When it comes to avoiding predators, bivalves have two main strategies. Infaunal bivalves bury themselves in the sand using a very strong muscular "foot." Epifaunal bivalves, meanwhile, attach themselves to rocks and can develop thick shells with strong spines.

details.notes: Photo caption reads 'Mussels attached to rocks' with label 'Bivalvia'. Photo credit: Colin Bates. Image shows mussels on rocks/sand. Grey rectangle in upper left corner.
Photo of a giant lion's paw scallop shell on black background. Photo credit: Randolph Femmer. Orange bar at bottom.

details.notes: Header panel for Bivalva: Veneroida section. Title reads 'Bivalva: Veneroida' with subtitle 'Clams and cockles'. Sidebar text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo of a common cockle shell. Photo credit: Feron Benjamin. Taxonomy tree with Veneroida highlighted in yellow. Orange bar at bottom.
Photo of a giant clam in underwater reef setting. Photo credit: Ryan Cloutier. Orange bar at bottom.

text.en: A local BC bivalve, the geoduck is the largest burrowing clam in the world, famous for digging very deep into the sand. It is also one of the most long-lived animals on Earth, with a life expectancy of about 150 years.

details.notes: Photo of a Pacific geoduck specimen on black background. Photo credit: Russell Docksteader. Orange bar at bottom.

Left portion of a two-part header panel for Cephalopoda section. Visible text: 'Cephalopoda' and 'Squids, octopuses, and'. Sidebar text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Title is cut off at right edge. Orange bar at bottom.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Mollusca > Cephalopoda

details.notes: Right portion of a two-part header panel for Cephalopoda section. Visible text: 'nautiluses'. Photo of a reef octopus. Photo credit: John Rix. Taxonomy tree with Cephalopoda highlighted in bold. Orange bar at bottom.

text.en: Cephalopods have an amazing ability to change colour and texture. This helps them not only camouflage themselves to avoid predators, but also show aggression or attract a mate.

details.notes: Photo of a reef cuttlefish in underwater setting. Photo credit: Nick Hobgood. Orange bar at bottom.
Photo credit: Lee Berger. Image shows a living nautilus with striped shell and tentacles visible.

taxonomy.tree: Animalia > Eumetazoa > Bilateria > Protostomia > Lophotrochozoa > Mollusca > Gastropoda

details.notes: Header panel for Gastropoda section. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Colin Bates.
Two photographs of the same species shown from different angles. Photo credit: Ryan Cloutier.

details.notes: Header panel for Gastropoda: Volutidae section. Text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo credit: Ria Tan.

text.en: Volutes are predatory sea snails with great appetites for other molluscs and echinoderms. They use their tongue-like radulas to penetrate openings in the shells of their prey and eat them from the inside out.

details.notes: Info panel for Volutes section. Photo credit: Richard Ling.

taxonomy.tree: Eukaryota > Rhodophyta > Rhodophyceae > Corallinales

details.notes: Header panel. Title reads 'Rhodophyta: Corallinales / Coralline algae'. Sidebar text reads 'Inside the cabinet'. Photo captioned 'Coralline rhodolith' credited to Artiom Shostak. Taxonomy tree displayed top-right.
Photo panel showing marine scene. Caption reads 'Graceful coral seaweed / Corallina vancouveriensis'. Photo credit: Colin Bates. No narrative text beyond caption.

text.en: Many coralline algae form crusts on rock surfaces. Each year some grow a new layer, about a third of a millimetre thick. Scientists in Alaska have found crusts that are 20 centimetres thick, estimated to be more than 700 years old!

details.notes: Photo of encrusting coralline algae on rock. Caption reads 'Rugose pink rock crust / Lithothamnion phymatodeum'. Photo credit: Colin Bates.

text.en: Researchers study coralline algal crusts like they do tree rings, to infer past global climate conditions such as ocean temperatures hundreds of years ago.

details.notes: Photo of Bossiella sp. growing on encrusting coralline. Caption reads 'Bossiella sp. and Rugose pink rock crust, Lithothamnion phymatodeum'. Photo credit: Colin Bates.
Blank dark panel with no visible text or specimen content.
Specimen photo showing multiple branching coralline algae. Caption reads 'Tenarea dispar on Macmillan's coral seaweed, Serraticardia macmillanii'. Photo credit: Artiom Shostak.

text.en: Corallines are not your typical red algae. Unlike other Rhodophyta, every single cell of a coralline alga is firmly encased in calcium carbonate, making them the hardest plants on the planet!

details.notes: Photo of branching red coralline algae. Caption reads 'Bead coral seaweed / Calliarthron tuberculosum'. Photo credit: Colin Bates.

Label reads 'Mesophyllum vancouveriense (on mussel)'. Photo credit: Artiom Shostak. Gray rectangle in upper left (possibly obscured label or adjacent panel edge). Two mussels shown with encrusting pink/white coralline algae.
Three species listed on a single label. Photo credit: Artiom Shostak. Two rock specimens shown with encrusting algae in green and pink/purple. Gray rectangle in upper left.

Photograph (not a museum specimen) of Turkish towel red algae in natural habitat. Photo credit: Colin Bates. Gray rectangle in upper left.

text.en: Constantinea is one of the longest-living fleshy algae known. Scientists have found specimens nearly 50 years old, but most only live 15 years or less.

details.notes: Specimen photograph of a red, perforated, leaf-like alga. Photo credit: Artiom Shostak. Narrative text displayed alongside specimen. Gray rectangle in upper left.
Second specimen photograph of Constantinea subulifera, showing red leaf-like fronds with dark holdfast region. Photo credit: Artiom Shostak. Gray rectangle in upper left.

text.en: Gelidium is a source of agar, which is often used to thicken or stabilize foods and industrial products. Scientists use it to grow bacteria and fungi, and you'll find it in some diet foods and desserts!

details.notes: Shows photograph of turf red algae (Gelidium pusillum) credited to D.S. Littler, and a circular inset photograph of agar credited to Unkky Panacek. Gray rectangle in upper left corner (likely display artifact or adjacent panel edge).

Large photograph of iridescent red seaweed (Mazzaella sp.) credited to Colin Bates. Gray rectangle in upper left corner.

text.en: Mastocarpus is heteromorphic, meaning it grows as different forms in different phases of its life cycle. In its gametophyte phase it is erect and blade-like. In its sporophyte phase, it is a crust that looks like tar spots on rocks.

details.notes: Photograph shows Petrocelis (labeled as 'crustose phase of Mastocarpus') on rocks, credited to Patrick Martone. Gray rectangle in upper left corner.
Dark/black panel with no visible text or specimen content. Gray rectangle in upper left corner. Green and blue horizontal bands at bottom edge.

text.en: Mazzaella contains carrageenan, which you'll find on the ingredient list of many products, including chocolate milk, ice cream, some cheeses, and toothpaste. Carrageenan thickens and stabilizes.

details.notes: Photo credit: Patrick Martone. Photo of seaweed in natural habitat with caption identifying species.
Dark/blank panel with no visible text or content. Blue and green horizontal bars at bottom edge.
Photo credit: Colin Bates. Close-up photograph of a red/coral-colored branching seaweed specimen. Scientific name caption visible below photo.
Two photographs of sea sac seaweed. Left photo credit: Patrick Martone. Right photo credit: Colin Bates. Shows yellow-golden sac-like structures.

text.en: In Japan, China, and Korea, some species of Porphyra are cultivated on nets to produce nori, a popular edible seaweed. Some BC First Nations also eat local Porphyra species, which the Squamish Salish call “lhék’es.”

details.notes: Photo credit: Patrick Martone. Shows leafy green seaweed specimens, possibly dried/preserved, with mussels visible in background.

text.en: Porphyra is heteromorphic, with a bladed or leafy phase alternating with a microscopic, filamentous phase that bores into barnacles and clamshells.

details.notes: Photo credit: Patrick Martone. Close-up of a single leafy Porphyra specimen. Continues the Porphyra/Nori information from the previous panel.

details.notes: Header panel for Rhodophyta / Red algae section. Photo credit: Artiom Shostak. Specimen image shows pink-red pressed algae fronds.

text.en: Many algal genera are named after people who studied algae. Can you guess the names of the people whom the following genera were named after: Smithora? Turnerella? Weeksia? Zinovaea?

details.notes: Info panel with interactive question about algal genus naming. Photo credit: Artiom Shostak. Specimen shows pink/purple pressed algae. Genera referenced: Smithora, Turnerella, Weeksia, Zinovaea.

text.en: The genus Smithora is named for G.M. Smith, author of Marine Algae of the Monterey Peninsula, Turnerella for D. Turner, an early 19th century British banker and phycologist, Weeksia for Mrs. J.M. Weeks, a California seaweed enthusiast in the late 19th century, and Zinovaea for A.D. Zinova, a Russian phycologist of the mid-20th century.

details.notes: Answer panel to the question posed in Face14_02. Photo credit: Patrick Martone. Specimen shows red algae close-up. Genera referenced: Smithora, Turnerella, Weeksia, Zinovaea.

text.en: Green algae (phylum Chlorophyta) get their name from their green photosynthetic pigment, chlorophyll. Red and brown algae also have chlorophyll, but they have other pigments that hide its colour.

Photo credit: Colin Bates.

text.en: Diatoms live almost everywhere that's wet, from the oceans to damp surfaces and from the poles to the tropics. The diatom Pseudo-nitzschia produces domoic acid, which is concentrated by shellfish and can cause gastrointestinal and neurological disorders in humans who eat them.

details.notes: Photo credit: Naoji Yubuki. Electron microscope image at 2,800x magnification with 10 um scale bar.
Dark/blank panel with no visible text or specimen content. Small gray rectangle in upper-left corner and green/blue stripe along bottom edge.

text.en: There could be up to 200,000 species of diatom, about a tenth of which have been described. Their silica cell walls are beautifully ornamented with many small holes. Fossil deposits of these hard silica shells, known as diatomaceous earth, are mined today for use in everything from dynamite to insecticides.

details.notes: Photo credit: Naoji Yubuki. Electron microscope image at 400x magnification with 5 um scale bar. Shows cylindrical diatom frustule.

text.en: Coralline algae live in every ocean on Earth, from warm Caribbean reefs to cold Alaskan waters. Corallines colonize bare rock, hold coral reefs together, and provide important habitat for many reef organisms.

details.notes: Photo credit: Colin Bates. Photo shows bead coral seaweed and California purple sea urchin.
Dark panel with no visible text or specimen labels. Blue and green horizontal bars at bottom.

text.en: When carbon dioxide accumulates in the atmosphere, some of it dissolves into the ocean, raising its acidity (decreasing its pH). In low-pH conditions, coralline algae can’t calcify and therefore can’t survive.

details.notes: Photo credit: Colin Bates. Photo caption identifies Bossiella sp.
Dark panel with no visible text or specimen labels. Blue and green horizontal bars at bottom.
Photo credit: Artiom Shostak. Specimen photograph with label identifying Graceful coral seaweed, Corallina vancouveriensis.

text.en: Coralline algae don’t appeal to herbivores — each bite is like a mouthful of rock! But corallines depend on herbivores to keep their surfaces clean of other algae and scum.

details.notes: Photo credit: Colin Bates. Photo shows Rugose pink rock crust (Lithothamnion phymatodeum) and Swirled pink rock crust (Pseudolithophyllum whidbeyense).
Photo credit: Colin Bates. Close-up specimen photograph of Bead coral seaweed, Calliarthron tuberculosum.

text.en: Some corallines have joints called genicula, made of soft tissues. Genicula are stronger, tougher, and stretchier than other fleshy seaweed tissues, and help erect corallines survive under crashing waves.

details.notes: Info panel with macro photo of Calliarthron cheilosporioides showing joints. Inset labeled 'Genicula 100x' shows microscopic view. Credit: Patrick Martone.

text.en: How does a calcified alga reproduce? Like other red algae, corallines can be male, female, or spore-producing sporophytes. In coralline species, these life phases all look similar.

details.notes: Info panel with two specimens shown. Left: 'Bead coral seaweed / Calliarthron tuberculosum / (male)'. Right: 'Bead coral seaweed / Calliarthron tuberculosum / (sporophyte)'. Credit: Patrick Martone.

text.en: Mature coralline fronds produce calcified, volcano-like swellings, called conceptacles, which hold the reproductive parts. These reproductive parts escape through pores in the conceptacle.

details.notes: Close-up photo panel showing conceptacles on Calliarthron tuberculosum. Caption reads 'Bead coral seaweed / Calliarthron tuberculosum / (showing conceptacles)'. Credit: Patrick Martone.

text.en: Bull kelp (Nereocystis) has a long, partially hollow, stem-like structure with a bulbous float on the end. Coastal First Nations used this float to store fish oil and water. Bull kelp can also be used as a trumpet!

text.en: Postelsia is a beautiful brown kelp that grows only on the most exposed rocky shores. This seaweed, which resembles a miniature palm tree, reaches half a metre in length at maturity in summer.

text.en: Sargassum muticum is a brown seaweed that grows in local waters but isn't native to our coast. It was accidentally introduced with young oysters from Japan when they were first farmed in the Strait of Georgia many decades ago.

details.notes: Photo of brown seaweed in water credited to David J Glaves. Caption reads 'Japanese seaweed / Sargassum muticum'. Blue/green strips at bottom edge.

text.en: The bryophytes include three groups of plants: mosses, liverworts, and hornworts. These plants are generally small, have no vascular systems or roots, and reproduce through spores rather than seeds.

details.notes: Three dried bryophyte specimens displayed with labels. Photo credited to Artiom Shostak. Yellow/green strips at bottom.

text.en: You'll find bryophytes in environments ranging from the tundra to the tropics, but they mainly live in moist, shady places. Some, however, grow in deserts, and even underwater.

text.en: Bryophytes have two life stages: the gametophyte stage, which produces the sex organs, and the sporophyte stage, which produces spores. Unlike other plants, however, the bryophyte lives longer in its gametophye stage than its sporophyte stage.

text.en: If you were to take a very close look at the “grass” in your yard, you’d likely find that it’s made up of bryophytes as well as grass. Common mosses found in lawns include Pseudoscleropodium purum and Rhytidiadelphus loreus.

text.en: Bryophytes on trees, rocks, and the forest floor blanket British Columbia’s temperate rainforest in a brilliant green. In fact, mosses and liverworts make up a big part of coastal forest biomass.

text.en: Mosses are the most diverse group of bryophytes, with approximately 10,000 species. A moss in its gametophyte stage is green and leafy. In its sporophyte stage, it usually grows short stalks topped with capsules full of spores.

text.en: Some bryophytes are still used in traditional Chinese medicine. Rhodobryum gigantum, for example, is sometimes used to treat cardiovascular problems.

text.en: Because some bryophytes only grow in very specific conditions, they can be excellent environmental indicators. Scientists can sometimes tell the acidity of a substrate just by looking at the bryophytes growing on it.

text.en: Two to three per cent of the Earth's surface is covered by the moss genus Sphagnum. These mosses are very absorbent—in fact, they can hold up to 20 times their weight in water!

text.en: The ability to absorb and store nutrients actually gives some bryophytes the ability to clean up toxic waste. Sphagnum, for example, is sometimes used to treat waste water containing heavy metals like iron and lead. It can also filter oils and dyes.

text.en: Unlike mosses, hornworts are not leafy. The hornwort’s gametophyte is called a thallus. It looks like a flat sheet, but may be lobed or a bit wrinkled. The hornwort’s spore capsules are tall “horns” that grow out of the thallus.

text.en: Hornwort sporophytes are unusual because they continue to grow and release spores all summer long. Unlike mosses, when the hornwort sporophyte is mature it splits down the middle, forming two long black "threads."

text.en: Liverworts grow in both thallose and leafy forms. You can tell leafy liverworts from mosses because their leaves grow in rows up the stem, while moss leaves grow in spirals. Leafy liverworts have oil bodies (liquid droplets inside their cells), and their sporophytes look different, too.

text.en: Spores must be dispersed for new plants to grow. Because the sporophytes of mosses, liverworts, and hornworts vary so much, they release spores in many different ways.

text.en: Liverworts' method of dispersing spores differs from other bryophytes. Inside their capsules, spores are attached to cells called elaters, which look like coiled-up springs.

details.notes: Informational panel about liverwort spore dispersal via elaters. Three circular magnified photos of Jungermannia sp. 'elaters' in italics.

specimens.notes: Magnified photographs of sporophyte; photo credit George Shepherd

text.en: When liverwort spores are mature and ready to be released, the elaters uncoil and "fling" the spores out of the capsule for the wind to carry away.

text.en: Lycophytes are one of the oldest living groups of vascular plants, arising more than 400 million years ago. Forests of tree-sized lycophytes dominated the landscape during the Carboniferous period. Their modern-day descendants, the club mosses, are much smaller.

text.en: If you are having trouble telling grasses, sedges, and rushes apart, remember this rhyme: "Sedges have edges, rushes are round, grasses are hollow, what have you found?"

text.en: Lichens are fungi and algae or cyanobacteria living in a close relationship, a symbiosis. The algae photosynthesize, making food. In some lichens, the fungus protects the algae from UV radiation. This lifestyle evolved separately many times!

text.en: Budding sunflowers are heliotropic. At sunrise, they face eastward. Throughout the day, they turn westward with the sun, then return to face eastward at night. When sunflowers bloom, they lose this ability to move with the sun.

text.en: The Precambrian spans 87 per cent of the Earth’s history. Over these billions of years the Earth saw great changes, including the emergence of cyanobacteria, which released oxygen into the atmosphere through photosynthesis.

details.notes: Info panel with photo of algae specimen. Credit: David Gilbar. Red bar along bottom.

text.en: The oxygen released by cyanobacteria destroyed the methane that was already in the atmosphere. Without it, global temperatures plummeted, causing a glacial period so cold that even the Equator was covered in ice. Scientists call this the “Snowball Earth” hypothesis.

details.notes: Info panel with photo of stromatolite specimen. Credit: Jens Rydell. Red bar along bottom.

text.en: The Devonian is known as the “Age of the Fish” because many new kinds of fish appeared, including the first sharks. Land-dwelling vertebrates also emerged in the Devonian. This period ended after a series of mass extinctions that wiped out as many as three-quarters of species.

text.en: Amphibians and insects thrived throughout the Carboniferous—and, in some cases, grew incredibly large. In fact, the largest known flying insect lived during the Carboniferous. Meganeura, as it is now called, looked like a modern dragonfly, except that it had a 75-centimetre wingspan! Very high levels of oxygen in the atmosphere helped insects like Meganeura grow so big.

text.en: Reptiles prospered during the Permian. Some pelycosaurs (scaleless reptiles) grew up to three metres long. The Permian ended with “the mother of all extinctions,” which may have killed over 95 per cent of species, including all trilobites as well as major groups of corals, brachiopods, and reptiles.

text.en: During the Triassic, all the Earth's continents were stuck together, forming one great supercontinent known as Pangaea. Modern corals appeared in the oceans, and the first dinosaurs emerged on land, along with flying reptiles and the first mammals. Near the end of the Triassic, another mass extinction allowed dinosaurs to become the dominant land vertebrates.

text.en: Over the course of these 43 million years, organisms began to look more like the forms we see today. Whales, bats, and horses emerged. Flowering plants diversified, and coral reefs flourished.

text.en: The period leading up to the present saw the appearance of animals we know today, including snakes, dolphins, rodents, and of course the Hominidae, or great apes. Modern humans did not appear until about 250,000 years ago, making us a tiny speck on the fossil record.

text.en: We can see how different populations of Sitka spruce were adapted to their home locales by studying how they grow once transplanted here in Vancouver. Trees from California, where the growing season is long, get bigger faster, while trees from Alaska grow slowly, but are hardier when it comes to surviving the cold. These differences are ingrained in the trees’ makeup and help them survive across their range.

details.notes: Top-right label reads: "Sitka spruce (trunk cross-sections) / Picea sitchensis / All specimens grown in Vancouver, BC". Illustration label: "Sitka spruce / Picea sitchensis". She studies whether BC's native trees can adapt to a warming climate." Map shows trunk cross-section specimens placed along Pacific coast from Alaska to California.

text.en: Underfoot in Vancouver's parks and ravines people have found fossils of ferns, conifers, flowering plants, and shells, some of which date as far back as 250 million years. The fossils you see here were found in Vancouver's neighbourhood of Kitsilano.

Second specimen catalog corrected from 2009-5738 to 2009-5736 a. Eocene age noted on Dryopteris label. Photo credit: Mari Chojiwa. Locality for all: Vancouver, BC.

text.en: Aquatic insects spend either part or all of their life cycles in water — or in some cases, skimming along its surface. Dragonflies, water striders, and backswimmers are just a few aquatic insects you’ll likely see at your local pond.

details.notes: Two-panel shadowbox. Upper panel shows above-water insects; lower panel shows underwater/surface insects. text.en: British Columbia boasts 2,101 species of moths, but only 184 species of butterflies. You’ve probably spotted common butterflies like the Lorquin’s Admiral, tiger swallowtail, and cabbage white flitting around Vancouver. Some BC butterflies, like the Taylor’s checkerspot (Euphydryas editha taylori), are disappearing fast from habitat loss.

text.en: Because mosses are so tiny, they can be easy to miss. But in British Columbia, more than 700 different species grow on tree trunks, along rooftops, and even in the cracks of sidewalks. A simple hand lens will reveal a tiny, beautiful plant world right under your feet.

Three circular inset photographs show moss specimens: two labeled Dicranum scoparium and one labeled Dicranum rugosum. Label at bottom-left reads "Dicranum moss / Dicranum fuscescens". text.en: Can you find two things that set these groups apart?

text.en: Animal life got really interesting really fast during the Cambrian. In fact, most animal diversity emerged then. Within five to ten million years — which seems long to you or me, but not to the Earth — all sorts of new creatures evolved. We call this huge increase in diversity the "Cambrian Explosion."

text.en:
Megalodon were gigantic sharks that roamed the oceans for thousands of years. But 2 million years ago, they went extinct. As the Earth got cooler, the warm waters that megalodon needed disappeared, and this may have brought about the end of the giant shark.

Megalodon could grow to 20 metres long — nearly as big as the Blue Whale skeleton here.

details.notes: Bottom of panel features a size comparison illustration showing megalodon (red) overlaid on a Blue Whale (grey).

specimens.notes: Echinoidea. Teaching collection. Multiple specimens displayed showing top, bottom, and various sizes.

text.en:
The five powerful teeth look like tiny doves, but they're tough enough to crush hard diatoms and even sand grains.

A living sand dollar looks fuzzy because it's covered in tiny spines, which it uses to burrow in sand. Underneath, it has five grooves lined with tube feet and cilia, which carry food to its mouth like a conveyor belt.

Sand dollars in their natural habitat.

details.notes: Label reads: Sand dollars, Echinoidea, Teaching collection. Small photo shows sand dollars in natural habitat. Inset circle at top right shows the five teeth (Aristotle's lantern). Multiple sand dollar specimens of various sizes displayed.

text.en:
Megalodons, the biggest sharks that ever lived, roamed the oceans 17 million years ago. A scientific controversy has raged for decades over whether the megalodons are more closely related to great whites or mako sharks. Scientists believe part of the answer is in the animals' teeth. Which of these shark teeth do you think resemble the megalodon's the most?

Man sitting on fossil restoration of Carcharodon megalodon jaws.

details.notes: Panel labeled S009 in bottom-right corner (appears to be part of a multi-panel megalodon exhibit with S009). Megalodon tooth label reads: Megalodon, Carcharodon megalodon, Teaching collection.

text.en: Millions of microscopic algae live symbiotically inside the tissues of coral polyps, giving the animals much of their colour. The algae get nutrients from the waste produced by the coral while playing a role in building the coral's calcium carbonate skeleton. But when corals get stressed, like many do when the ocean warms, they eject their algae and die. This is called "coral bleaching." Corals' single-celled algal symbionts are called zooxanthellae.

details.notes: Two labeled specimen groups (not three as originally extracted). First label covers two specimens: Tropical corals / Anthozoa / No. MI4215 and No. MI4216. Previous third NULL/NULL species entry removed as miscount. Images by Todd LaJeunesse.

text.en:
For thousands of years, local First Nations peoples have harvested clams, mussels, abalone, and other molluscs to eat. They used the shells in art and clothing, such as carvings, masks, pendants, ceremonial shawls, and as items for trade.

Tusk shells from western Vancouver Island were used as currency by the Yurok of California.

details.notes: Seven mollusc shell specimens displayed, representing species used by local First Nations peoples.

specimens.notes: Unionidae. Displayed open showing nacreous interior.
Five buttons made from unionid mussel shell.
Part of periostracum removed to reveal mother of pearl.

text.en:
Snails, clams, mussels, and other molluscs need their shells. But collectors often take living molluscs when shells are at their finest. Decades of worldwide trade have promoted overharvesting, especially in tropical areas. This means fewer molluscs as food for other animals and humans, and has led to extinctions and endangered ecosystems.

Land snails are among the most endangered animals on Earth.

details.notes: Six species displayed illustrating shell trade and overharvesting. Bullmouth helmet has visible cameo-style carving.

specimens.notes: Growth series of approximately 9 shells arranged in a spiral pattern from small to large.

text.en:
Abalones are flattened sea snails. Like all molluscs, they start out as eggs and then hatch into tiny microscopic larvae with a token shell. As snails grow they add new material to the edge of their shells.

The larva of many molluscs, including abalones, swims freely in the water and is called a veliger.

details.notes: Inset diagram shows a veliger larva at 0.5mm scale. Shells arranged in growth series spiral.

text.en: Carrier snails like to decorate. They glue shells and other objects to themselves, probably for extra protection or camouflage. These snails hold each treasure against their shell's growing edge and then secrete calcium carbonate to cement it into place. To test the hold, they gently rock back and forth. They then remain still to allow the shell to bond. Shells placed upside down look empty and unsatisfying to hungry predators.

details.notes: Five specimens now identified (previously only 3). Three Xenophora pallidula (Japan) with catalog numbers MI4149, MI4056, MI4134. One Xenophora sp. (MI4058). One Xenophora robusta (West coast of Mexico, MI1841). All catalog numbers now resolved. Specimen count increased from 3 to 5.

specimens.notes: Many cone snail shells displayed in a spiral arrangement and in rows; family Conidae, Marine Invertebrate Collection. Individual species not labeled.

text.en: Cone snails' poisonous, barbed harpoons spear prey like fish and worms, paralyzing them. Some cone snail venom is strong enough to kill a person.

details.notes: Label reads: Cone snails / Conidae / Marine Invertebrate Collection. Illustrations by Derek Tan show cone snail hunting sequence with fish. Numerous cone snail shells displayed in spiral pattern and vertical row. Illustrations credited to Derek Tan.

text.en:
Snails are beautiful escape artists. Because speed isn't an option, they've developed different types of shells to help avoid predators. For instance, slippery shells keep crabs from gaining a grip, spiny shells are tricky for fish to bite, narrow openings restrict access to snails' soft parts, periscope-like shells protect extended body parts, and hard shells act like armour against attack.

A conch can jump straight up into the water using its powerful foot, and Turritella can hide up inside its long shell.

details.notes: Eight species displayed illustrating diverse shell defense strategies.

text.en: What do snails, slugs, clams, and squids have in common? Like all molluscs, they come from the same ancestor, which lived more than 500 million years ago. This mollusc "family tree" shows how they're all related.

details.notes: Phylogenetic tree diagram showing eight mollusc classes: Aplacophora (illustration only), Polyplacophora (Chitons, specimen displayed), Monoplacophora (illustration only), Rostrochonchia (extinct, no specimen), Scaphopoda (Tusk shells, specimen displayed), Bivalvia (Mussels, clams, and cockles, specimen displayed), Gastropoda (Snails and slugs, specimen displayed), Cephalopoda (Squids, octopuses, and cuttlefish, cuttlefish bone displayed). Illustrations by Derek Tan.

text.en:
The mantle is a nifty piece of mollusc anatomy. It creates all the different shell shapes you see. The mantle edge is where new shell grows in layers with the help of glands. A mollusc uses its prismatic gland and, when present, the periostracum gland to build the shell's outer layers, while its mantle gland forms the pearly inner layer.

Shells have growth bands that form over time like tree rings.

details.notes: Includes anatomical cross-section diagram of shell formation showing: Chalky prismatic layer, Pearly nacreous layer, Mantle, Mantle gland, Periostracum gland, Prismatic gland, Skin-like periostracum layer. Two Turbo marmoratus specimens shown to compare periostracum intact vs mother-of-pearl exposed.

specimens.notes: Multiple sea star specimens of various species displayed; label reads: Sea stars / Asteroidea / Zoology Collection. Individual species not labeled.

text.en: The powerful suction of sea stars' tube feet allows these mostly carnivorous animals to tightly grasp their prey — some can even force open clam shells.

details.notes: Approximately 10-12 sea star specimens of varying sizes, colors, and arm counts displayed. Label: Sea stars / Asteroidea / Zoology Collection. Small illustration of a walrus at bottom left.

specimens.notes: Five brittle star specimens displayed in separate mounting boxes; label reads: Brittle stars / Ophiuroidea / Stein Collection. Specimens show regenerating arms.

text.en:
Our skin heals when we cut it, but imagine extending this ability to regrowing whole fingers, hands — arms even! That's why researchers are busy studying echinoderms like starfish and brittle stars. These animals can regenerate whole chunks of their bodies that get severed.

Someday, research on how brittle stars regrow body parts, like the ones here are doing, might lead to human organ regeneration.

details.notes: Five brittle star specimens mounted in separate gray boxes, showing various stages of arm regeneration. Label: Brittle stars / Ophiuroidea / Stein Collection.

text.en: Bivalves — molluscs with two-part shells, such as clams and oysters — have colonized one of the most prolific habitats on Earth: sandy and muddy water bottoms. By looking closely at the size and strength of a bivalve's shell, siphon, and foot, you can tell whether it burrows beneath the sand, sits on the bottom in moving waters, or attaches to rocks to keep from floating away.

details.notes: All six bivalve specimens now fully identified. Four previously NULL scientificNames resolved: Malleus albus (white hammer oyster), Euvola ziczac (zigzag scallop), Siliqua patula (Pacific razor clam), Brechites attrahens (watering pot shell). Panopea abrupta common name resolved to Pacific geoduck. Interpretive captions per specimen: pen shell — byssal threads info; hammer oyster — wedged between coral reef rocks; scallop — iceberg method; razor clam — smooth surface for rapid burrowing; watering pot — lives buried in muddy sand; geoduck — siphon burrows to nearly one metre.

text.en: You'll find molluscs in coral reefs, sandy shorelines, deep oceans, rainforests, and almost everywhere in between. Estimated at 200,000 species, molluscs may be the second most diverse animal group on the planet, after arthropods. Mollusc evolution has led to amazing variety, from fleshy to shelled, rainbow-coloured to camouflaged, poisonous to harmless, gorgeous to creepy.

details.notes: Ten mollusc shell specimens displayed showcasing diversity. All labels clearly legible with catalog numbers.

specimens.commonName: Sea stars, sea urchins, and sea cucumbers

text.en: What is an animal? Vertebrates, such as fish, frogs, birds, and humans, are all animals, but so are insects, worms, molluscs, and many more creatures. Animals have to eat to get their energy—they can't get it straight from the sun like plants do. Most (but not all) animals have muscle and nerve cells.

details.notes: Overview panel of animal phyla. Mix of specimen photographs and illustrations representing 17 phyla. No individual catalog numbers visible.

specimens.notes: Two specimens: one whole shell, one cross-section showing internal chambers

text.en: As a chambered nautilus grows, it closes off "rooms" in its shell and builds newer, bigger ones. By pumping air and fluid into these chambers through tiny tubes, the nautilus can make itself move up and down in the water. With up to 90 tentacles and two simple eyes, the chambered nautilus is related to squids and octopuses.

details.notes: Two nautilus shell specimens displayed alongside a line drawing illustration of a living nautilus. Catalog numbers listed as No. M14021 and No. M1022. Illustration credit appears to read 'Diane Tuz' or similar.

text.en: Today's cephalopods are mostly squishy, which is to say, they don't leave much in the way of bones behind when they die. Take an octopus, for example. After its body decomposes, all that remains is the hard beak this cunning predator uses to eat. Only a few modern cephalopods make hard outer shells like the nautilus does, though many, like squids, have a hard structure inside for support. Ammonites and belemnites were hard-shelled cephalopods that were abundant until they went extinct 65 million years ago.

details.notes: All six cephalopod specimens now fully identified. Three previously NULL scientificNames resolved: Spirula spirula (ram's horn squid), Coleoidea (belemnite, Eagle Butte, South Dakota), Ammonitida (ammonite). Nautilus sp. corrected to Nautilus pompilius (species level). Octopus specimen is specifically the beak. All catalog numbers now resolved. Photo credit: Mari Chojiwa.

text.en: Snails build their own shells. Hermit crabs don't. But both need shells to survive. So what's going on? As snails grow, they create larger shells. When they die and leave intact shells behind, hermit crabs adopt these ready-made homes, trading smaller shells for bigger ones as they grow.

details.notes: Display shows relationship between snail shells and hermit crabs. Diagram shows hermit crab + whelk shell = hermit crab in shell. Multiple hermit crab specimens in various states displayed.

text.en: Malaria started out hundreds of millions of years ago as a harmless microscopic alga, which later evolved into the mosquito-borne parasite that plagues us now. Understanding this evolutionary history led to the discovery that malaria still carries plant-like genetic material, and has prompted scientists to search for a treatment based on the herbicides that we use to kill weeds.

details.notes: Features researcher Patrick Keeling, a professor in UBC's Department of Botany researching the origin and evolution of single-celled protists, including parasites that live inside cells and cause diseases like malaria. Photo credit: Nick Wiebe. University of British Columbia, 2010. Mosquito family name Culicidae and catalog number E.0399 now confirmed via zoom. Chromera velia described as 'a brown alga and close relative of Plasmodium.' Plasmodium vivax micrograph credited to Wellcome Images.

text.en: The algae below look so similar that they were originally labelled as one species. But DNA evidence has now placed them in three different species. The study of organisms' DNA has shown us that many things that look the same, like these algae, are actually different... ...and many things that look different are in fact the same. The algae below all belong to one species — a newly discovered one, yet to receive a name.

details.notes: Upper section shows three Mastocarpus specimens from different clades that look similar but are genetically distinct. Lower section shows four algae specimens of varying morphology that belong to one undescribed species. Lower specimen labels too small to read reliably. Researcher bio: Dr. Sandra Lindstrom, adjunct professor at UBC's Department of Botany, researches red seaweed and other algae from the coast of California to Alaska. University of British Columbia, 2010.

text.en: Clayoquot First Nations people used bull kelp, a brown seaweed that grows to more than 60 feet long in a year, for many different purposes. They traditionally used dried kelp for fishing lines, as medicines for children, and even as firecrackers — the dried floats explode when thrown in the fire.

details.notes: Researcher bio: Dr. Louis Druehl is a professor of marine botany at Simon Fraser University. He researches algal diversity and how it is affected by human disturbances. Simon Fraser University, 2010.

specimens.notes: A packet of nori seaweed is displayed as a physical object

text.en: Some bacteria have special powers. Researchers found intestinal bacteria in people in Japan that can digest seaweed carbohydrates that most gut bacteria can't. The researchers think this comes from eating sushi: some time in the past, Japanese gut bacteria stole a gene from another microbe that lives on nori seaweed. Microbes can trade genes the way people can give each other books or tools, a process called "horizontal gene transfer."

details.notes: Diagram shows horizontal gene transfer from seaweed bacterium to Japanese gut bacterium. Silhouette figures illustrate prevalence. Researcher bio: Jan-Hendrik Hehemann is a marine glycobiologist at the University of Victoria. He coauthored a paper that described this transfer in gut bacteria. University of Victoria, 2010.

text.en: Not all skeletons are made of bones. Organisms have independently evolved countless ways of supporting their bodies. Skeletons can be inside or outside the body, jointed or rigid, massive or microscopic, and based on calcium, silicon, or carbon. The fossils of microscopic skeletons help geologists determine the age of rocks.

details.notes: Comparative anatomy display showing skeleton diversity across many phyla. Multiple physical specimens displayed in lower section along with microscope images in upper section.

specimens.notes: 2008, Hopkins Marine Station, Pacific Grove, California

text.en: Lignin, meaning "wood" in Latin, is the stuff that gives plant cell walls the strength to sprout upwards. Scientists thought it evolved to give land plants the strength to hold themselves up in air, and so researchers were surprised to find lignin in a wave-battered red seaweed. This discovery suggests aquatic algae had lignin over a billion years ago, before the ancestors of land plants split off from the red algal line.

details.notes: Two specimen sheets displayed showing pressed red coralline algae. Researcher bio: Patrick T. Martone is an assistant professor in UBC's Department of Botany. He studies the evolution of macroalgae and the properties of algal cell walls. University of British Columbia, 2009.

text.en: Most coralline algae grow flat on rocks. About 100 million years ago, some corallines began to branch upright into the water, braving the intense currents and crashing waves. These erect corallines produced strong, flexible joints, called genicula, which allow the fronds to bend without breaking.

details.notes: Central specimen sheet shows erect branching coralline. Three loose specimens (rocks/shell with pink coralline crusts) are displayed around the sheet.

text.en: The specimens at left show one of the two forms of liverworts; scientists call it thalloid. The other form, a leafy liverwort, is at right. Unlike mosses and hornworts, liverworts grow fleshy, short-lived sporophytes. Can you see the tiny cups on the second specimen? Inside the cups are gemmae, tiny discs that get splashed out by raindrops and grow into new liverworts.

details.notes: Illustrated diagram at left shows thalloid liverwort anatomy including archegoniophores, sporophyte, and gemmae cup. Three physical specimens displayed. Diagram labels visible: Archegoniophores, Sporophyte, Gemmae cup.

specimens.notes: Labeled: June 13, 2011; Point Grey, Vancouver, BC

text.en: Hornworts look like black grass. The blades of "grass" are actually reproductive structures; distinctive photosynthetic "horns" that produce spores. Unlike the many thousands of moss species, there are only about 100 known species of hornworts. Hornworts are a type of bryophyte, or non-vascular plant, different from mosses and liverworts.

details.notes: Illustration of hornwort plant accompanies specimen photo. Catalog number reads No. E.0540.

text.en: An easy way to tell if something's a moss is by what it's not. Mosses are bryophytes, or non-vascular plants, which means they don't move water around with roots and stems. Instead, they absorb water and nutrients through their leaves, and they just anchor themselves with root-like rhizoids. Mosses don't have flowers or produce seeds. Instead, they reproduce via spores, fragmentation, and gemmae (single cells) or brood bodies (groups of cells) that break off to form new plants.

details.notes: Includes moss life cycle diagram with stages: Spores germinate and grow into a new moss plant, Male antheridia, Sperm swims to female, Female archegonia, Fertilized eggs develop into gametophytes and sporophytes, Spore dispersal. Also includes label for 'Cure green seaweed Monostrop' (partially illegible, top left specimen label). One specimen top-left labeled 'Cure green seaweed / Monostrop' — this appears to be from an adjacent or overlapping display and may be misplaced context.

text.en: This species of moss absorbs pollutants. The concentrations of heavy metals in this moss have been used to monitor air quality in the Fraser Valley. It's a "bioindicator": an organism that provides information about the conditions in its environment. Isothecium is very common in wooded areas. This specimen was collected from trees lining Main Mall at UBC.

details.notes: Scientific name partially legible on label; reads 'Isothecium stoloniferum' based on visible characters. Includes close-up photo of moss on tree bark and a photo of tree-lined Main Mall at UBC. Catalog number reads No. E.0171. The bottom-right corner has the S041 identifier but is mostly cut off.

text.en: An alga is an aquatic organism that photosynthesizes, but doesn't have roots like a land plant. Some algae are single cells and can swim through the water, while others are big and fastened to the ocean bottom -- like giant kelp, which can be 200 feet long and creates underwater forests.

details.notes: Multiple algae types shown. Top-left green specimen label partially illegible. Red alga specimen (Phycodrys isabellae) has readable label with catalog No. A.0101. Some labels are small and partially legible.

text.en: Some mosses have tiny "teeth" at the openings of their capsules to protect their spores. They open and close depending on heat and moisture. New research shows that early mosses lacked these peristome teeth in their capsules, so peristome teeth probably evolved later in moss evolution. The plants used in this research are kept here in the museum. The genus Polytrichum is known for its numerous peristome teeth attached to a central membrane. Spores fall out through the openings between the teeth.

details.notes: Features researcher profile: Ying Chang, PhD student in UBC's Department of Botany (University of British Columbia, 2010). She uses the DNA of land plants to investigate evolutionary history. Large macro photo credited to Daniel Cotter. Smaller photos credited to Jolene Vroom.

text.en: Pale green Oregon beaked moss forms a luxurious carpet on coastal forest floors and is a common moss on the ground in Pacific Spirit Regional Park. Can you see the prominent "beak" it was named for?

details.notes: Large magnified macro photo of single capsule showing the characteristic beak. Dried specimen displayed at right. Catalog number reads No. E.0366. Photo credit partially legible, appears to read 'Derek Tan'.

text.en: This moss looks like little trees, but they're all connected underground. The moss puts out horizontal underground runners, like strawberries. These produce more "trees," allowing the mosses to colonize new space by cloning, a form of asexual reproduction.

text.en: Mosses play an important role in rainforest ecosystems. They soak up water and nutrients like a sponge, and they may not release them back into the ecosystem. Mosses also provide shelter and food for many insects and arthropods, both important parts of the food web.

details.notes: Rainforest moss ecology panel. Features a large photo of a mossy forest scene. Four moss specimens displayed with labels. Some label details too small to confirm with certainty.

specimens.notes: Shown in close-up photo at top right with sporophyte structures; label partially legible
Label reads: Cheung Road, BC; No. E.0406 a-d. Four small specimens shown on slug illustration

text.en: Mosses reproduce by spores or fragmentation, or by using specialized structures called gemmae and brood bodies, which break off from the main plant. Spores are usually transported by wind, but sometimes insects help to move them around. Gemmae, brood bodies, and moss fragments are also distributed by wind or water, or by hitching a ride on animals.

details.notes: Moss reproduction panel. Features an illustration of a fly at top left and a slug at bottom carrying moss fragments. Close-up photo of Splachnum sporophyte. Four small Dicranum specimens displayed on the slug illustration. Also includes No. B17000 visible near Splachnum label.

text.en: Mosses of the Aleutian Islands were a passion for Wilf Schofield, who spent 15 years collecting there every summer. The Aleutians are special because they used to be part of a land bridge from North America to Asia. Studying the plants there helps us understand how plants came to live where they do today. Wilf Schofield (1927-2008), professor emeritus at UBC, was a celebrated bryologist. To understand and know bryophytes, you had to actually study them in their natural habitat.

details.notes: Biographical/geographic panel about Wilf Schofield's Aleutian Islands moss research. Features a map of Alaska with red location markers. Multiple herbarium sheets with labels from 'University of Alaska, U.S.A.' are displayed but individual species names are largely illegible at this resolution. A portrait photo of Schofield appears at bottom left with credit 'University of British Columbia, 2008'. No individual species can be reliably extracted from the herbarium labels.

specimens.notes: Label reads: Pacific sphagnum (with sporophytes); Sphagnum pacificum; July 19, 2010; Camosun Bog, Pacific Spirit Park, BC; No. E.0317 a,b

text.en: As the spore capsules dry out their shape changes from spheres to cylinders, until the round cap pops off and the capsule explodes. Sphagnum mosses shoot their spores up into the air, where the wind blows them to new sites. Their "gun" is a ball-shaped capsule, filled with spores. As the capsule dries out the pressure increases until finally the capsule blows its top, shooting out the spores.

details.notes: Sphagnum spore dispersal panel. Features a macro photograph of sphagnum sporophytes (green stems with dark capsules) at top left. Dried specimen at top right. A sequence of illustrations at the bottom shows the capsule drying and exploding stages. Large silhouette of spore cloud in reddish-brown. Photo credit partially visible: 'Ivar Leidus'.

specimens.notes: Label reads: Dung moss; Splachnum ampullaceum; Adak Island, Alaska; No. B17000. Small specimen visible at left beneath close-up photo

text.en: Home is a pile of dung for over half of the moss family Splachnaceae. Dung doesn't last forever, so these mosses must find new dung for their offspring. Flies are attracted by the odours these mosses secrete, then disperse the plants' sticky spores to fresh dung.

details.notes: Dung moss ecology panel. Features a close-up photo of a Splachnum sporophyte (reddish-purple). Three circular illustrations show fly-mediated spore dispersal. An illustration of dung at the bottom. Family Splachnaceae is mentioned in the narrative text.

text.en: Moss matters to people. It's important not only in ecosystems but also to the commercial flower industry, which pays for moss collected in the wild. But many mosses are sensitive to light and grow very slowly. In many places, moss has been extracted faster than it can regenerate, a practice some people call "moss mining."

details.notes: Moss conservation/commercial use panel. Three labeled moss specimens displayed. A photograph at bottom shows trays of commercially collected moss. Four moss clumps visible total (one unlabeled at top right).

text.en: Prison inmates at Cedar Creek Correctional Centre in Washington State are working in a laboratory to learn how to grow moss. Many mosses take a very long time to grow back after being harvested, so growing them in prisons could help conserve wild populations. Studying mosses can prepare inmates for jobs when they are released. Dr. Nalini Nadkarni teaches forest ecology at the Evergreen State College in Washington. Her research in mosses led her to develop a conservation project in correctional centres.

details.notes: Moss conservation/prison program panel. Four labeled moss specimens displayed. Chain-link fence pattern in background. Photo of Dr. Nalini Nadkarni at bottom left (credited Evergreen State College, 2011). Photo of an inmate studying moss at bottom right (credited Nalini Nadkarni). Panel describes the Cedar Creek Correctional Centre moss-growing program.

text.en: This moss's silvery appearance comes from tiny "hairs" on the tips of the leaves that reflect sunlight and keep the wind from drying it out. Its compact growth form helps keep water in. These adaptations help it colonize dry habitats, such as Vancouver's cement curbsides and bridges. Usually bright green, the leaves of this moss curl up and look brown when it's dry, making it appear "tortured" — like its name. This is another way of conserving moisture.

details.notes: Two moss species displayed. Top half features Grimmia with close-up photo and magnified views. Bottom half features Tortula with close-up photo and dried specimens in a dark inset box.

text.en: If there were only girls left on the planet, humans would have something in common with Takakia lepidozioides. Male plants have never been found, and are thought to have gone extinct during an ice age. The female plants reproduce asexually. Takakia is called "impossible moss" because its mix of liverwort and moss features made it impossible to classify for decades.

details.notes: Single species panel. Large magnified image of Takakia branch shows forked leaf structure. Small specimen container image at center.

specimens.notes: Label reads: Jan 5, 2021; UBC campus, Vancouver, BC. Catalog number partially illegible (starts with E). Autumn-coloured pressed leaves displayed across upper portion.

text.en: Imagine a living building with plants growing on its walls. Vegetation can help keep buildings cool in the summer and warm in the winter — saving money and resources. The living walls, a green roof, and a biofiltration system at UBC's Centre for Interactive Research on Sustainability (CIRS) make it one of the greenest buildings in the world.

details.notes: Panel about green buildings. Photo of CIRS building at UBC shown. Campus map displayed on right side showing building locations. Bottom text identifies Alberto Cayuela as the associate director for the UBC Sustainability Initiative. University of British Columbia, 2013.

Two microscope images of spores shown at 100x and 400x magnification. Labeled as Glomus claroideum (spores). Referenced in context of fungal association with moonwort.

text.en: It helps to have friends in low places — if you're a largely subterranean plant like moonwort, that is. These ferns can live completely underground for years, thanks to their association with fungi. The fungi connect moonwort to other plants' roots and divert sugars to the underground plant. Moonwort's underground lifestyle makes it hard for conservation scientists to know if populations are a healthy size.

details.notes: Panel about subterranean ferns and mycorrhizal fungi. Features a full herbarium specimen sheet of Botrychium virginianum with color calibration card. Microscope images of fungal spores (Glomus claroideum) shown at two magnifications.

specimens.notes: Herbarium sheet with bulb, leaves, and flowering parts. Catalog number V137131 visible on sheet. Also shown in photo (top right) with purple flowers.

Shown in photographs (middle right and bottom right) with white flowers and blue camas for comparison. Bottom label reads: Death camas, Toxicoscordion venenosum, June 13, 2015, location partially illegible (appears to reference Spruce Bridge, BC). Catalog number illegible.

text.en: Delicious food or deadly poison? Common camas and death camas often grow side by side, and look almost the same when they are not flowering. The bulbs of common camas were an important food source for First Nations peoples on the Pacific coast. But the lookalike bulbs of death camas are deadly: a single bulb can kill a human adult. Death camas bulbs contain a poisonous alkaloid chemically similar to strychnine, but more potent.

details.notes: Panel comparing edible common camas with poisonous death camas. Herbarium sheet shows Camassia quamash with bulb. Decorative flower motifs along bottom edge.

text.en: Nearly all life on Earth relies on energy from sunlight. Plants, algae, and many bacteria harness the sun's rays with pigments: molecules that absorb light. Pigments like chlorophyll use the sun's energy to change water and carbon dioxide into sugars and oxygen, trapping energy in chemical bonds for later use. Most living things that can't live on sunlight still consume products of photosynthesis — by eating other organisms and breathing oxygen.

details.notes: Panel about photosynthesis. Three plant species displayed with light rays illustrated from above. Includes diagram of chloroplast showing chlorophyll. Multiple pressed plant specimens arranged artistically.

specimens.notes: Label reads: Common cordgrass, Spartina anglica, date partially illegible, Boundary Bay, BC. Catalog number partially illegible. Full plant displayed showing roots, stem, and leaves.

text.en: Non-native cordgrass can quickly devastate mudflats and beaches, so to predict the next invasion, researchers launched "drift cards" at existing invasion sites. The cards floated like the cordgrass seeds, and they carried a phone number for citizen-scientists to report sightings. Knowing where the cards landed helped researchers know where to look for new invasions.

details.notes: Panel about invasive cordgrass. Full plant specimen displayed with visible root system. Orange 'Research Cooperation' drift card shown on driftwood at top. Bottom left identifies Dan Buffett as a regional biologist for Ducks Unlimited Canada who works to protect and restore wetlands and other waterfowl habitat along the BC coast.

specimens.notes: Whole plant displayed with roots showing nodules; label text partially legible, reads 'Clover / Trifolium sp.'; collection location appears to include 'Food Botany, Washington'
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria referenced in narrative text as living in clover root nodules

text.en: These clover roots might look infected, but the nodules are actually home to beneficial bacteria. Rhizobium "fix" nitrogen by converting nitrogen from the air into a form that plants can use. The plants benefit, and when they die and decompose, they act as natural fertilizer. Nitrogen-fixing plants, including many plants in the legume family, are part of traditional crop rotation systems that enhance soil fertility.

details.notes: Diagram shows atmospheric nitrogen (blue molecules above soil line) being converted to ammonium (available for plant use) below soil line. Small label near plant partially legible.

specimens.notes: Branch with lobed leaves displayed at right side; small label reads 'Garry oak / Quercus garryana' with collection info partially legible, appears to include 'Vancouver, BC'

text.en: Most oaks are deciduous, which means their leaves turn colour and are shed each year, but some oaks keep their leaves year-round. These are called "live" or "evergreen" oaks, an umbrella term for the various species of oak that keep their leaves. This is an adaptation to very dry environments, where it is costly for a plant to replace all its leaves at once. Live oaks have evolved multiple times in dry climates in North America, Europe, and Asia. Of the more than 500 species of oaks worldwide, about 30 are evergreen or "live," like this Garry oak.

details.notes: Phylogenetic tree diagram in center shows distribution of live oaks across regions: North America, North America and Europe, Europe and Asia, Europe. Colored dots indicate lineages.

specimens.notes: Historical herbarium sheet displayed at left; handwritten labels partially legible. Label on right reads 'Pacific willow / Salix lucida / (also lasiandra)' with additional collection info partially legible

text.en: Pacific willow lives on sunny riverbanks from California to Alaska and as far east as Saskatchewan. Willow flowers are borne in catkins, long columns of flowers that turn into fuzzy mixtures of seed capsules and soft, cottony down that helps the seeds disperse by wind.

details.notes: Herbarium sheet at left shows pressed willow specimens with multiple handwritten labels (mostly illegible at this resolution). Fresh pressed branch displayed at right. Photo of researcher Diana Percy at bottom left with text about her research on 'bar codes' for willows at the Beaty Museum. Gray lines at right suggest wind/seed dispersal. Color calibration chart visible at top of herbarium sheet.

text.en: Plants in the mustard family, like wasabi, defend themselves from herbivores with chemicals so powerful they can't store them in their own cells. Instead, they keep two harmless molecules in separate compartments. One bite brings the two together and activates the bomb.

details.notes: Stylized graphic background shows plant cell compartments with colored shapes (red, green, yellow) representing chemical defense molecules. Location marker 'S070' visible at bottom right.

text.en: Ever thought of planting a garden on your roof? The vegetation keeps the building warm, and provides a habitat for small creatures to live in. There's one growing right above your head, on the museum's green roof -- one of several at UBC.

text.en: Bunchberry flowers are spring-loaded. Their stamens are held together under tension. When an insect lands on the tiny flowers, they release, flinging pollen at the pollinator.

details.notes: Left column shows sequential white line illustrations of the flower opening mechanism from closed bud to pollen release. Upper left shows insect landing on flower with magnifying lens effect. Multiple pressed bunchberry specimens at various growth stages displayed on right. Location marker 'S073' visible at bottom right.
